paras: The killing of Charles Dew was the death of a Black farmer in Riley Township, Clinton County, Michigan, who was found hanging in his granary with his head laid open in late August 1881, months after masked men had tarred and feathered him. Early dispatches tied his death to his attempt to prosecute the tarring party, and several papers called it a lynching. One member of the tarring party later confessed and named seven others, but the only murder trial, of Dew's wife and her brother Ben Cooper, ended in acquittal in 1882.

Dew, a "colored farmer" whose first name was also printed Charley, Chester and Chesley, had lived for many years in southern Clinton County. Wire reports said he lived alone, and one added that "the popular complaint" was that he had cruelly treated and driven off his wife. Der Nordstern, a German-language paper in St. Cloud, Minnesota, called him a tyrant to his family who abused his livestock, and the True Northerner later wrote that this cruelty had made him "universally detested."

According to the Lansing dispatch, masked men visited him "last spring" and gave him a coat of tar and feathers. Der Nordstern said neighbors broke into his house for the tarring and threatened to kill him if he did not change. Days before his death, he went to St. Johns, the county seat, to begin legal proceedings against those he believed responsible.

Dew was killed on the night of Tuesday, August 23, 1881. In Der Nordstern's account, his wife was away, and around midnight the Coopers, relatives by marriage living nearby, heard him cry "Mord, Mord" (murder). Cooper refused his wife's plea to help, because Dew had accused him of joining the tarring; the next morning he found Dew hanging from a beam in the barn, and neighbors gathered and cut the body down.

The Lansing dispatch reported a gash in the left side of the head "evidently made by an axe," while Der Nordstern described wounds over the right eye and at the back of the head and abrasions pointing to a hard struggle. It concluded that he was stunned by a blow and probably dead before he was hanged. The New York World added a dislocated leg, the True Northerner said he was bound hand and foot, and one news column said he was "hanged and riddled with bullets by a mob."

In mid-September, Michigan papers reported that A. W. Burrett had confessed to taking part in the tarring and implicated seven others. The Lake County Star added that the murder itself was "still shrouded in mystery."

Suspicion eventually fell on Ben Cooper, "another colored man" living on the Dew farm, and on Dew's wife, Cooper's sister. Their trial at St. Johns, postponed several times, lasted two weeks in a term that closed in spring 1882. The evidence was entirely circumstantial, and the jury acquitted them.

The Lansing dispatch of August 26 ran as "Probable Murder by Hanging" in the New-York Tribune, "A Persecuted Man" in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and "An Outrage" in the Somerset Herald. Other editors cast it in Reconstruction terms: a Daily Gazette headed it "Kualuxism [Kukluxism] in Michigan," and the Washington Evening Star "An Outrage by Michigan Kuklux." Weekly news columns cut the story to a few sentences and disagreed about Dew, one calling him "quarrelsome" and abusive to his wife, another saying he had many enemies but was not quarrelsome.

The New York World used the case for a partisan jab at Republicans, deploring violence in "the lawless North" and mocking calls to protect "the harmless colored man"; Democratic papers in Ohio and Pennsylvania reprinted it. Der Nordstern headed its account "Ein Lynchgericht in Michigan" and called the killing evidently a lynching, while dwelling on the neighbors' grievances.

Accounts differed on who killed Dew: the early dispatches and Der Nordstern linked the death to the tarring party, while the 1882 prosecution targeted his own household. Reports also disagreed on whether he lived alone and whether he was shot, and placed the tarring "last spring," "several days" before the death, or apparently in August.

reader.title: Killing of Charles Dew
bases: Dew, earlier tarred and feathered by a masked band, was found beaten and hanged in his granary, and several papers called it a lynching by a mob (A1, A9, A10, A14), though the only prosecution charged two members of his household with murder (A17).

The Lansing wire report, the independent German-language account and a later Michigan trial report agree that Dew was found dead hanging in his barn or granary with head wounds after being tarred and feathered (A1, A6, A14, A17); who killed him is disputed.

accounts.label: Der Nordstern (German-language)
accounts.gist: Neighbors angered by his treatment of family and stock had tarred him and threatened to kill him; on Tuesday night, with his wife away, he was stunned and hanged in his barn after a struggle, and a relative who heard his cries refused to help.

accounts.label: Michigan state news
accounts.gist: Burrett confessed to the tarring and named seven others, but the murder remained a mystery.

accounts.label: Trial report
accounts.gist: Ben Cooper and Dew's wife were tried at St. Johns for the murder on circumstantial evidence and acquitted.

framing.detail: The Lansing dispatch ran under 'Probable Murder by Hanging', 'A Persecuted Man' and 'An Outrage', linking the death to his lawsuit against the tarring party.
Headlines 'Kualuxism in Michigan ... Brained With an Ax and Hanged' and 'An Outrage by Michigan Kuklux' cast it as Klan-style violence in the North.
The 'Tragical Tales' column reported the murder alongside the claim that Dew 'was quarrelsome and had abused his wife'.
The N. Y. World, reprinted by Democratic papers, used the 'brutally lynched' farmer to mock Republican 'bloody shirt' appeals for protecting 'the harmless colored man'.
Der Nordstern called it plainly a lynching but described Dew as a family tyrant whose neighbors were justly indignant.
The True Northerner reported the acquittal, repeating that Dew's cruelty had made him 'universally detested'.
